record.title: D'Alembertian
record.name: DAlembertian
record.content:
The D'Alembertian is the equivalent of the Laplacian in Minkowskian geometry. It is given by: \[ \Box = 
abla^2 -  rac{1}{c^2}  rac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2} \] Here we assume a Minkowskian metric of the form $(+, +, +, -)$ as typically seen in special relativity. The connection between the Laplacian in Euclidean space and the D'Alembertian is clearer if we write both operators and their corresponding metric. \subsection{Laplacian} \[ \mbox{Metric: } ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 \] \[ \mbox{Operator: } 
abla^2 =  rac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} +  rac{\partial^2}{\partial y^2} +  rac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2} \] \subsection{D'Alembertian} \[ \mbox{Metric: } ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 -cdt^2 \] \[ \mbox{Operator: } \Box =  rac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} +  rac{\partial^2}{\partial y^2} +  rac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2} -  rac{1}{c^2} rac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2} \]
In both cases we simply differentiate twice with respect to each coordinate in the metric. The D'Alembertian is hence a special case of the generalised Laplacian. \section{Connection with the wave equation} The wave equation is given by: \[ 
abla^2 u =  rac{1}{c^2} rac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} \] Factorising in terms of operators, we obtain: \[ (
abla^2 -  rac{1}{c^2} rac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2})u = 0 \] or \[ \Box u = 0 \] Hence the frequent appearance of the D'Alembertian in special relativity and electromagnetic theory. \section{Alternative notation} The symbols $\Box$ and $\Box^2$ are both used for the D'Alembertian. Since it is unheard of to square the D'Alembertian, this is not as confusing as it may appear. The symbol for the Laplacian, $\Delta$ or $
abla^2$, is often used when it is clear that a Minkowski space is being referred to. \section{Alternative definition} It is common to define Minkowski space to have the metric $(-, +, +, +)$, in which case the D'Alembertian is simply the negative of that defined above: \[ \Box =  rac{1}{c^2}  rac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2} -
abla^2 \]
